title: Fuel blockades bring the country to a halt
context: Hauliers and farmers blockade oil refineries over high fuel duty. Petrol stations run dry and the protesters demand an immediate tax cut.
reality: In September 2000 blockades emptied petrol stations. Tony Blair refused to cut duty under pressure; Gordon Brown's November pre-budget report froze fuel duty and cut vehicle excise duty for lorries and small cars.
choices: Fund public transport and fuel-saving help
Freeze duty and offer targeted relief
Hold firm and leave prices unchanged

title: The Millennium Dome money pit
context: The flagship millennium attraction draws far fewer visitors than forecast and needs fresh public money to stay open through the year.
reality: The Dome drew about 6.5 million visitors against a 12 million target. The Millennium Commission granted extra Lottery money several times in 2000 while a buyer was sought; it closed on 31 December 2000.
choices: Inject fresh public funds to keep it running
Grant limited extra funds and seek a buyer
Close it early and cut the losses

title: Who may read the nation's emails?
context: Email and mobile phones are spreading fast. Police and intelligence agencies want clear legal powers to intercept communications and obtain data.
reality: The Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 put interception, communications data and covert surveillance on a statutory footing, with ministerial warrants, oversight commissioners and a tribunal.
choices: Grant broad powers to intercept and monitor
Grant powers under warrants and oversight
Leave it to providers and existing law

title: A ten-year plan for the NHS
context: Winter crises and long waiting lists strain the health service. The Prime Minister has promised to raise health spending towards the European average.
reality: The March 2000 Budget raised NHS funding by over 6% a year in real terms. The NHS Plan of July 2000 promised 7,000 extra beds, 7,500 more consultants and 20,000 more nurses.
source: Department of Health, The NHS Plan (2000)
choices: Fund a large multi-year NHS expansion
Fund targeted increases tied to reforms
Hold spending and encourage private care

title: Foot-and-mouth disease sweeps the countryside
context: A highly contagious livestock disease spreads across farms. Footpaths close, rural tourism collapses and farmers demand action and compensation.
reality: Over 6 million animals were slaughtered in 2001; the army helped with disposal and local and general elections were delayed to June. The NAO put the cost at about £3bn to the public sector and £5bn to the private sector.
choices: Mount a mass cull with army help and compensation
Combine targeted culls with vaccination
Leave containment to farmers and councils

title: After 11 September
context: Terrorist attacks in the United States kill nearly 3,000 people. Washington prepares military action against al-Qaeda and its Taliban hosts in Afghanistan.
reality: Tony Blair pledged to stand 'shoulder to shoulder' with the US. British forces joined strikes on Afghanistan from 7 October 2001, and Britain led the first ISAF security mission in Kabul.
choices: Join military action with substantial forces
Offer limited support and push UN diplomacy
Stay out of military action

title: Emergency anti-terror powers
context: After the attacks abroad, the security services warn of foreign terror suspects in Britain who can be neither deported nor prosecuted.
reality: The Anti-terrorism, Crime and Security Act 2001 allowed indefinite detention without trial of foreign terror suspects. In December 2004 the Law Lords ruled this incompatible with human rights law.
source: House of Lords judgment, A v Home Secretary (2004)
choices: Allow detention without trial
Expand surveillance but keep trials
Rely on existing criminal law

title: Riots in northern towns
context: Violent clashes involving white and Asian youths and the police erupt in Oldham, Burnley and Bradford, exposing deeply segregated communities.
reality: After the summer 2001 riots the government commissioned the Cantle Report, which found communities living 'parallel lives' and made community cohesion a national policy priority.
choices: Fund major regeneration and integration schemes
Commission a review and fund cohesion projects
Leave it to the police and local councils

title: Paying for the NHS
context: An independent review warns that the health service needs years of higher funding. The Treasury must decide how to pay for it.
reality: In the April 2002 Budget, following the Wanless review, Gordon Brown raised National Insurance by one percentage point from April 2003 to fund large increases in NHS spending.
choices: Raise national insurance to fund the NHS
Fund modest rises through growth and borrowing
Hold spending and keep taxes unchanged

title: Firefighters walk out
context: The firefighters' union demands a 40% pay rise. Strikes loom, and the army's ageing 'Green Goddess' engines would have to provide cover.
reality: Firefighters struck from November 2002 while troops provided emergency cover. The dispute ended in June 2003 with a 16% rise over three years, tied to modernisation of the service.
choices: Fund the full pay demand
Offer a phased rise tied to reform
Refuse talks and rely on army cover

title: The Sangatte camp at Calais
context: Hundreds of migrants at a Red Cross centre near Calais try nightly to reach Britain through the Channel Tunnel. France wants a deal.
reality: Britain and France agreed to close Sangatte in December 2002; Britain admitted about 1,200 of its residents. The 2003 Le Touquet treaty then placed British border checks on French soil.
choices: Fund joint border operations and resettlement
Negotiate closure in exchange for some intake
Refuse any intake and leave it to France

title: What to do after Railtrack
context: The privatised rail infrastructure company has collapsed into administration after fatal crashes and spiralling costs. The network needs a new owner.
reality: Railtrack was put into administration in October 2001. In October 2002 the network passed to Network Rail, a not-for-dividend company whose debts were backed by the state.
choices: Fully renationalise the rail network
Create a not-for-dividend public-interest firm
Sell it to new private investors

title: War in Iraq
context: The United States is preparing to invade Iraq over alleged weapons of mass destruction. A second UN resolution looks out of reach and huge crowds march in protest.
reality: On 18 March 2003 the Commons backed military action by 412 to 149, after 139 Labour MPs rebelled on an amendment. British forces joined the invasion two days later; no WMD stockpiles were found.
choices: Join the invasion with major forces
Back action only with a new UN mandate
Refuse to take part in the war

title: Should the pound join the euro?
context: The Treasury has set five economic tests for joining the single currency. The assessment is due and business is divided.
reality: In June 2003 Gordon Brown announced that only one of the five tests, on financial services, had been met. Britain would not join the euro for now; the question was never revived.
choices: Prepare to join the euro
Keep the option open and review later
Rule out euro membership

title: Charting Britain's energy future
context: North Sea output is past its peak and climate commitments loom. Ministers must set a long-term direction for power supply.
reality: The 2003 Energy White Paper set a goal of cutting carbon dioxide emissions by about 60% by 2050 and backed renewables, but left new nuclear power as an option without committing to it.
choices: Fund renewables and new nuclear stations
Set climate goals, keep nuclear option open
Leave the energy mix to the market

title: Freedom for top hospitals
context: Ministers propose giving the best-performing NHS hospitals more independence over finances and pay. Many MPs fear a two-tier health service.
reality: The Health and Social Care Act 2003 created NHS foundation trusts. The key Commons vote in November 2003 passed with a majority of just 17.
choices: Keep central control and fund more
Grant autonomy to top-rated hospitals
Open the NHS widely to private providers

title: Opening the doors to new EU members
context: Ten countries join the EU in May. Most existing members restrict workers from the new states for years; Britain must choose its approach.
reality: Britain, Ireland and Sweden gave immediate labour market access in May 2004, with a worker registration scheme. A study had forecast 5,000-13,000 net arrivals a year; actual inflows were far higher.
choices: Open the labour market and fund integration
Open access with worker registration
Impose transitional controls for years

title: Top-up tuition fees
context: Universities say they are underfunded. The government proposes variable fees repaid after graduation, despite an earlier pledge not to introduce them.
reality: The Higher Education Bill passed its second reading by just 316 to 311 in January 2004. Variable fees of up to £3,000 a year began in 2006, repayable after graduation.
choices: Fund universities from general taxation
Introduce deferred fees with grants
Let universities set market fees

title: The hunt for efficiency savings
context: Public spending has risen fast. A review proposes cutting back-office costs and civil service posts to free money for frontline services.
reality: The 2004 Gershon Review identified £21.5bn of annual efficiency gains by 2007-08, and the government planned to cut about 84,000 civil service posts.
choices: Keep expanding services and staff
Make phased savings and reinvest them
Cut deeply to lower spending

title: Workers lose their pensions
context: Thousands of workers have lost much of their pensions after employers with underfunded schemes went bust. They demand protection.
reality: The Pensions Act 2004 created the Pension Protection Fund from April 2005, financed by a levy on defined-benefit schemes rather than taxpayers. A separate Financial Assistance Scheme helped earlier victims.
choices: Fund a taxpayer-backed pension guarantee
Create a lifeboat fund paid by schemes
Leave it to employers and trustees

title: Bombs on London's transport network
context: Suicide bombers attack three Underground trains and a bus in London, killing dozens. Police want far longer pre-charge detention.
reality: The 7 July 2005 bombings killed 52 people. The government sought 90-day pre-charge detention but lost a Commons vote in November 2005; the Terrorism Act 2006 set 28 days.
choices: Seek 90-day detention and tough new powers
Extend detention moderately, add offences
Rely on existing counter-terror laws

title: Make Poverty History
context: Britain hosts the G8 summit at Gleneagles. Campaigners and global concerts demand debt relief and more aid for Africa.
reality: At Gleneagles in July 2005 the G8 endorsed cancelling the debts of 18 of the poorest countries and pledged to raise aid by around $50bn a year by 2010.
choices: Lead a big push on aid and debt relief
Agree targeted debt relief only
Avoid new spending commitments

title: The pensions time bomb
context: People are living longer while saving too little. A commission proposes reforming state and private pensions for decades ahead.
reality: The Turner Commission reported in 2005. The Pensions Acts of 2007 and 2008 restored the earnings link, raised the state pension age to 68 by 2046 and introduced automatic enrolment into workplace pensions.
choices: Raise the state pension, funded by taxes
Pair a later pension age with auto-enrolment
Leave retirement saving to individuals

title: MG Rover collapses
context: The last big British-owned volume carmaker runs out of money after talks with a Chinese partner fail. Thousands of jobs at Longbridge are at risk.
reality: MG Rover collapsed in April 2005 with around 5,000-6,000 job losses. Ministers declined a bailout beyond a £6.5m bridging loan and announced a £150m package for workers and suppliers.
choices: Nationalise or bail out the carmaker
Fund retraining and help for suppliers
Let it collapse without intervention

title: National identity cards
context: The government wants biometric ID cards and a national identity register to fight terrorism, fraud and illegal working. Civil liberties groups object.
reality: The Identity Cards Act 2006 created the National Identity Register and biometric cards. The scheme was abolished by the Identity Documents Act 2010 before it was widely rolled out.
choices: Build a national ID card and register
Introduce voluntary ID cards only
Drop the ID card plans

title: A new generation of nuclear power?
context: Ageing nuclear and coal plants will close within two decades while gas imports grow. Ministers must decide whether to back new nuclear stations.
reality: The 2006 Energy Review and the 2008 Nuclear White Paper backed new nuclear power, on condition that private companies would fund, build and operate the stations.
choices: Fund new nuclear stations with public money
Allow private nuclear build without subsidy
Leave the power mix to the market

title: Foreign prisoners freed without deportation checks
context: It emerges that over a thousand foreign prisoners were released without being considered for deportation. Some cannot be traced.
reality: In 2006 the Home Office admitted that 1,023 foreign prisoners had been freed without deportation checks. Charles Clarke was sacked, and in 2007 the department was split, creating the Ministry of Justice.
source: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee
choices: Overhaul and split the Home Office
Tighten deportation rules and review cases
Fix it within existing budgets

title: Smoking in pubs and restaurants
context: Scotland is banning smoking in enclosed public places. The government must decide how far a ban in England should go.
reality: Ministers first proposed exempting private clubs and pubs not serving food, but MPs voted 384 to 184 in February 2006 for a full ban, which took effect in England in July 2007.
choices: Ban smoking in all enclosed public places
Ban it with exemptions for some pubs and clubs
Leave smoking rules to venues

title: A run on Northern Rock
context: A mortgage lender reliant on wholesale funding has asked the central bank for emergency support. Savers queue to withdraw their money.
reality: In September 2007 Britain saw its first bank run in well over a century. Alistair Darling guaranteed Northern Rock's deposits; when no private buyer was found, it was nationalised in February 2008.
choices: Nationalise the bank immediately
Guarantee deposits and seek a buyer
Let the bank fail

title: Summer floods
context: Exceptional rain floods towns across England. Homes are ruined, and a failed water treatment works leaves hundreds of thousands without tap water.
reality: The summer 2007 floods killed 13 people and flooded about 55,000 properties; the Mythe works failure cut supplies to some 350,000 people. Flood defence spending was raised and the Pitt Review commissioned.
choices: Fund major new national flood defences
Raise flood spending and review resilience
Leave protection to insurers and councils

title: Restoring power-sharing in Northern Ireland
context: Devolved government in Northern Ireland has been suspended since 2002. The two largest parties remain far apart, but talks are progressing.
reality: After the 2006 St Andrews Agreement, Ian Paisley and Martin McGuinness became First Minister and deputy First Minister on 8 May 2007, restoring devolved government.
choices: Fund a large peace and investment package
Broker power-sharing with firm deadlines
Continue direct rule from London

title: 25 million records lost in the post
context: The tax authority has lost two discs holding the child benefit records of millions of families, including bank details.
reality: In November 2007 HMRC admitted losing two CDs with data on 25 million people. Its chairman resigned, and reviews led to new data-handling rules across government.
choices: Fund an overhaul of state data security
Order reviews and tighten data rules
Leave departments to fix their own systems

title: The banking system on the brink
context: Global credit markets have frozen after a US investment bank collapsed. Several major British banks could fail within days.
reality: In October 2008 the government announced a £500bn rescue: £50bn to recapitalise banks, £250bn of loan guarantees and £200bn of liquidity. RBS and Lloyds-HBOS received about £37bn of state capital.
choices: Recapitalise banks with public money
Guarantee lending and broker mergers
Let failing banks go under

title: Recession: a fiscal stimulus?
context: The economy is shrinking and unemployment rising. Economists debate whether the government should borrow to boost demand.
reality: In November 2008 Alistair Darling cut VAT from 17.5% to 15% for 13 months, at a cost of about £12.5bn, and brought forward some capital spending.
choices: Fund a big public investment programme
Bring forward projects and target support
Cut VAT tax temporarily to lift spending

title: 42 days without charge
context: Police argue that complex terror plots need longer pre-charge detention. Critics call it an attack on civil liberties.
reality: The Commons approved 42-day detention by just nine votes in June 2008, but the Lords rejected it by 309 to 118 in October and the government dropped the plan.
choices: Extend detention to 42 days
Allow extension only in emergencies
Keep the 28-day limit

title: A legally binding climate target
context: Campaigners demand binding cuts in emissions. Business fears higher energy costs during a downturn.
reality: The Climate Change Act 2008 made an 80% cut in greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 legally binding, with five-year carbon budgets and an independent Committee on Climate Change.
choices: Legislate binding targets and carbon budgets
Set non-binding targets with reviews
Leave emissions to markets and the EU

title: The MPs' expenses scandal
context: Leaked records show MPs claiming for second homes, moat cleaning and a duck house. Public anger at politicians is intense.
reality: The Daily Telegraph's revelations from May 2009 forced Speaker Michael Martin out. The Parliamentary Standards Act 2009 created the independent IPSA, and an audit ordered repayments.
choices: Create an independent regulator and audit all
Tighten the rules and order repayments
Leave reform to Parliament itself

title: Car industry in free fall
context: Car sales have collapsed in the recession. Manufacturers and dealers ask for state help as plants cut shifts.
reality: The 2009 Budget launched a car scrappage scheme: £2,000 off a new car when trading in one over ten years old, half paid by the state and half by manufacturers.
choices: Fund large direct bailouts for carmakers
Fund a targeted scrappage incentive
Leave carmakers to the market

title: Reinforcements for Helmand
context: British casualties in Afghanistan are at their highest. The United States is sending a troop surge and asks allies to do more.
reality: 2009 was the deadliest year for British forces in Afghanistan. Gordon Brown agreed to send 500 more troops, taking the total to about 9,500, on conditions including equipment and allied contributions.
choices: Send substantial reinforcements
Send limited troops with conditions
Begin withdrawing British forces

title: A record deficit
context: Borrowing has soared to its highest level since the Second World War. The government must choose between stimulus, tax rises and cuts.
reality: Alistair Darling's April 2009 Budget created a 50p top income tax rate from April 2010, funded the Future Jobs Fund and set out a plan to halve the deficit over four years.
choices: Keep stimulus going and fund job schemes
Raise the top tax rate, phase deficit cuts
Start deep spending cuts now

title: A coalition and the deficit
context: A new coalition government takes office facing a record peacetime deficit. With the Greek debt crisis unfolding, ministers must set a fiscal course.
reality: The June 2010 emergency Budget raised VAT to 20%, and the October Spending Review cut departmental budgets by an average of 19% over four years.
choices: Delay cuts and keep investing
Phase in consolidation, mixing taxes and cuts
Front-load deep spending cuts

title: Tripling tuition fees
context: Funding for university teaching is being cut. An independent review proposes higher fees repaid through income-contingent loans.
reality: In December 2010 MPs voted 323 to 302 to raise the fee cap to £9,000. The Liberal Democrats, who had pledged to oppose any rise, split, and student protests turned violent.
choices: Fund universities through general taxation
Raise fees with income-linked repayments
Cut teaching grants and lift the fee cap

title: Defence review in an age of austerity
context: The defence budget faces a large black hole while troops fight in Afghanistan. Expensive programmes must be cut or protected.
reality: The 2010 Strategic Defence and Security Review cut the defence budget by 8% in real terms over four years, retired the Harrier jets and HMS Ark Royal, and scrapped the Nimrod MRA4.
choices: Protect the defence budget in full
Trim spending, keep core programmes
Make deep cuts to help close the deficit

title: One benefit to replace six
context: The benefits system is complex and can leave people better off out of work. Ministers propose a single, digitally run payment.
reality: The November 2010 white paper proposed Universal Credit, merging six means-tested benefits. The Welfare Reform Act 2012 enacted it, but the rollout ran years behind schedule.
choices: Build a single new digital benefit
Simplify existing benefits step by step
Just cut existing benefits

title: Riots spread across English cities
context: After a fatal police shooting in Tottenham, looting and arson spread across London and other cities for several nights.
reality: The August 2011 riots left five people dead. 16,000 police were deployed in London, courts sat through the night, and the Troubled Families programme followed in December.
choices: Fund large youth and family programmes
Surge police numbers and fast-track courts
Leave recovery to the police and councils

title: Protecting civilians in Libya
context: Libya's dictator sends his forces against rebel-held Benghazi and threatens a massacre. France and Britain push for a no-fly zone.
reality: After UN Security Council Resolution 1973, the RAF joined strikes on Libya in March 2011. The Commons backed action by 557 votes to 13; Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown that year.
choices: Lead air strikes to enforce a no-fly zone
Back sanctions and support allies
Stay out of the conflict

title: A treaty to save the euro
context: Eurozone leaders want EU treaty changes for tighter budget rules. Britain wants safeguards for its financial services sector.
reality: In December 2011 David Cameron vetoed an EU-wide treaty change after failing to secure safeguards for the City. The other states agreed the Fiscal Compact as a separate treaty.
choices: Join the new fiscal treaty
Accept changes in return for safeguards
Veto the treaty change

title: Public sector pensions strike
context: Ministers want public employees to work longer and pay more into their pensions. Unions call a mass walkout.
reality: Unions said up to two million public sector workers struck on 30 November 2011. Following the Hutton review, final-salary schemes were replaced by career-average schemes and contributions rose.
choices: Keep current schemes and fund the cost
Move to career-average schemes with protection
Close the schemes to new staff

title: Security for the Olympic Games
context: Weeks before the London Olympics, the private security contractor admits it cannot supply enough guards for the venues.
reality: In July 2012 G4S failed to deliver enough guards; the government deployed 3,500 extra troops at short notice, and the Games passed off securely.
source: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee
choices: Deploy troops to fill the gap
Mix extra police with contractor staff
Leave the contractor to fix it

title: Regulating the press after phone hacking
context: A judicial inquiry into phone hacking recommends an independent press regulator backed by law. Newspapers warn of state control.
reality: The Leveson Report of November 2012 called for statutory underpinning. David Cameron refused; instead a Royal Charter on press self-regulation was agreed in 2013.
choices: Legislate for a statutory press regulator
Back a Royal Charter-based regulator
Leave the press to regulate itself

title: The 50p top tax rate
context: The 50p top rate of income tax is said to raise little and deter investment. Cutting it in hard times could look unfair.
reality: George Osborne's March 2012 Budget cut the top rate to 45p from April 2013. U-turns on a 'pasty tax' and other measures led critics to call it an 'omnishambles'.
choices: Keep 50p and fund more investment
Keep the top rate for now, review later
Cut the top income tax rate

title: Capping benefits
context: Ministers argue that no workless household should receive more in benefits than the average working family earns.
reality: The Welfare Reform Act 2012 introduced a £26,000 annual household benefit cap from 2013, with exemptions for disabled people, alongside the so-called 'bedroom tax' in social housing.
choices: Protect benefits and fund more housing
Cap benefits with exemptions
Cut benefits across the board

title: Chemical weapons in Syria
context: The Syrian regime is accused of a nerve-gas attack near Damascus that killed hundreds. The United States plans punitive strikes.
reality: On 29 August 2013 the Commons rejected the government's motion on military action by 285 to 272. David Cameron accepted the result and Britain did not join strikes.
choices: Join punitive military strikes
Push the UN route and humanitarian aid
Stay out of any action

title: Hinkley Point C
context: No new nuclear plant has been built for decades. A French state-owned firm will build one only with a long-term guaranteed price.
reality: In October 2013 the government agreed a strike price of £92.50/MWh for 35 years with EDF for Hinkley Point C. The project has since run years late and far over budget.
source: Department of Energy and Climate Change
choices: Build new nuclear with public money
Guarantee a price for private builders
Leave new plants to the market

title: Getting first-time buyers on the ladder
context: Young people struggle to raise deposits, and housebuilding is weak after the crash.
reality: The 2013 Budget launched Help to Buy, offering equity loans of up to 20% on new-build homes and mortgage guarantees. Critics said it pushed up prices.
choices: Fund a large public housebuilding drive
Subsidise buyers with equity loans
Leave housing to the market

title: Equal marriage
context: Same-sex couples can form civil partnerships but cannot marry. Religious groups are divided over change.
reality: The Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 legalised same-sex marriage in England and Wales from March 2014, with protections for religious bodies that decline to conduct such marriages.
choices: Legislate full marriage equality
Legalise it with religious protections
Keep civil partnerships only

title: Scotland decides
context: Scotland will vote on independence. Days before the vote, a poll puts the Yes side ahead for the first time.
reality: Unionist party leaders pledged extensive new powers in 'The Vow'. On 18 September 2014 Scotland voted 55.3% No; the Smith Commission led to the Scotland Act 2016.
choices: Pledge sweeping new powers for Scotland
Offer a negotiated devolution package
Refuse further concessions

title: Data retention struck down
context: Europe's top court has annulled the EU data retention directive. Police warn they will lose access to phone and internet records.
reality: The Data Retention and Investigatory Powers Act was rushed through Parliament within days in July 2014, with a sunset clause for the end of 2016 and an independent review.
choices: Pass a permanent law expanding retention
Pass a temporary law with a sunset clause
Let data retention lapse

title: Russia annexes Crimea
context: Russian forces have seized Crimea and are stoking conflict in eastern Ukraine. Allies debate how hard to punish Moscow.
reality: Britain backed EU and G7 sanctions, and Russia was suspended from the G8. After flight MH17 was shot down over eastern Ukraine in July 2014, sanctions were tightened.
choices: Push maximum sanctions and arm Ukraine
Coordinate targeted EU sanctions
Avoid measures that hurt trade

title: The Rotherham abuse report
context: An inquiry finds that about 1,400 children in one town were sexually exploited over 16 years while officials failed to act.
reality: The 2014 Jay report found around 1,400 children were abused in Rotherham between 1997 and 2013. After the Casey inspection, ministers sent commissioners to run the council in 2015.
choices: Launch a national inquiry and fund victims
Inspect and take over the failing council
Leave it to local agencies

title: Europe's refugee crisis
context: Over a million people head for Europe, many fleeing war in Syria. The EU wants member states to share asylum seekers through quotas.
reality: Britain stayed out of EU relocation quotas. In September 2015 David Cameron pledged instead to resettle 20,000 Syrian refugees directly from the region over five years.
choices: Accept large numbers under EU quotas
Resettle refugees directly from camps
Take no additional refugees

title: Air strikes against ISIS in Syria
context: After deadly terror attacks in Paris, France asks allies for help. British jets already strike ISIS in Iraq, but not in Syria.
reality: On 2 December 2015 the Commons voted 397 to 223 to extend RAF air strikes against ISIS into Syria.
choices: Extend air strikes into Syria
Keep to Iraq, support allies otherwise
Stay out of further military action

title: A national living wage
context: Low pay is widespread and in-work benefits are costly. The Treasury considers a much higher legal wage floor.
reality: The July 2015 Budget announced a National Living Wage of £7.20 an hour for over-25s from April 2016, with the aim of reaching 60% of median earnings by 2020.
choices: Raise the wage floor sharply
Raise it gradually on expert advice
Leave wages to the market

title: Cyber attacks on the rise
context: Hackers target companies and public bodies, stealing data on millions of customers. The security agencies want more money and a national cyber centre.
reality: In November 2015 George Osborne announced £1.9bn over five years for cyber security and a new national cyber centre; the National Cyber Security Centre opened in 2016.
choices: Fund a national cyber security centre
Fund targeted protection for key systems
Leave cyber defence to companies

title: In or out of the EU?
context: Pressure grows for a public vote on EU membership. The Prime Minister has renegotiated some terms and must decide whether and how to put the question to the people.
reality: David Cameron held an in/out referendum on 23 June 2016 after renegotiating membership terms. Leave won with 51.9% and Cameron resigned.
choices: Hold an in/out referendum
Renegotiate and let Parliament decide
Refuse a referendum

title: The 'snoopers' charter'
context: Emergency data laws expire soon. Intelligence agencies want powers for bulk data collection and to require storage of internet connection records.
reality: The Investigatory Powers Act 2016 authorised bulk interception and required providers to keep internet connection records for 12 months, with warrants approved by judicial commissioners.
choices: Legislate broad bulk surveillance powers
Grant powers with judicial approval
Let emergency powers lapse

title: Steel in crisis
context: Cheap imports and high energy costs hit steelmaking. The owner of the country's largest steelworks, at Port Talbot, puts its UK business up for sale.
reality: Tata Steel announced in March 2016 that it would sell its UK business. Ministers ruled out nationalisation but offered to co-invest up to 25% alongside a buyer; Tata ultimately kept the business.
source: Department for Business, Innovation and Skills
choices: Nationalise the steelworks
Offer co-investment to a buyer
Let the market decide

title: A levy on sugary drinks
context: Child obesity is rising. Health campaigners call for a levy on sugary soft drinks; the industry warns of job losses.
reality: The 2016 Budget announced the Soft Drinks Industry Levy, in force from April 2018, with revenue initially used for school sport. Many manufacturers cut sugar to avoid it.
choices: Impose a sugar levy and fund school sport
Negotiate voluntary sugar cuts
Leave diets to consumers

title: Fire at Grenfell Tower
context: A fire in a London tower block kills dozens. Flammable cladding is then found on hundreds of buildings across the country.
reality: The Grenfell Tower fire of 14 June 2017 killed 72 people. A public inquiry followed; in 2018 the government funded £400m to remove cladding from social housing, with private blocks funded later.
choices: Fund cladding removal on all buildings
Fund social-housing work and review rules
Leave remediation to building owners

title: A wave of terror attacks
context: Attacks hit Westminster, a pop concert in Manchester and London Bridge within months. The national threat level is raised to critical.
reality: The 2017 attacks killed 36 people, 22 of them at Manchester Arena. Troops were briefly deployed under Operation Temperer, and the Counter-Terrorism and Border Security Act 2019 followed.
choices: Deploy troops and toughen terror laws
Review strategy and boost police resources
Rely on existing police powers

title: Triggering Article 50
context: After the referendum, the government must formally notify the EU of withdrawal and decide what kind of future relationship to seek.
reality: Theresa May triggered Article 50 on 29 March 2017, having ruled out single market and customs union membership in favour of a bespoke, deep free trade agreement.
choices: Seek to stay in the single market
Seek a bespoke free trade deal
Prepare to leave on WTO terms

title: Rip-off energy tariffs
context: Millions of loyal customers pay far more than those who switch supplier. Consumer groups demand a cap on prices.
reality: The government legislated in 2018 for a cap on default energy tariffs, which the regulator Ofgem introduced from January 2019.
choices: Cap all energy tariffs by law
Cap default tariffs only
Leave prices to competition

title: Nerve agent attack in Salisbury
context: A former Russian spy and his daughter are poisoned with a military-grade nerve agent in an English city. Moscow denies involvement.
reality: Britain expelled 23 Russian diplomats in March 2018 and allies expelled over 150 more. A local woman, Dawn Sturgess, died that July after exposure to discarded Novichok.
choices: Impose sweeping sanctions on Russia
Expel diplomats and rally allies
Limit the response to protests

title: The Windrush scandal
context: Long-settled Caribbean-born residents have been wrongly denied jobs, healthcare and benefits, and some deported, for lacking documents.
reality: The scandal broke in April 2018 and Home Secretary Amber Rudd resigned. The government apologised, offered citizenship and set up a compensation scheme in 2019.
choices: Fund full redress and end hostile policies
Apologise, regularise status, compensate
Review cases one by one

title: A birthday present for the NHS
context: The NHS turns 70 amid long waits and winter crises. Its leaders call for a multi-year funding settlement.
reality: In June 2018 Theresa May announced NHS England funding would rise by £20.5bn a year in real terms by 2023-24, about 3.4% a year, followed by a ten-year Long Term Plan.
source: Department of Health and Social Care
choices: Fund a large multi-year NHS increase
Fund modest rises tied to efficiency
Hold spending and expand private care

title: Carillion collapses
context: A giant contractor that runs services in hospitals, schools and prisons faces insolvency and asks for state support.
reality: Carillion went into compulsory liquidation in January 2018. The government refused a bailout; the Official Receiver kept public services running with state funding.
choices: Bail out the contractor
Ringfence key contracts with interim support
Let it go into liquidation

title: Brexit deadlock
context: Parliament has rejected the withdrawal agreement three times. The EU grants delays and a no-deal exit is a real possibility.
reality: After record defeats for Theresa May's deal, Boris Johnson renegotiated it in October 2019, replacing the Irish backstop with the Northern Ireland Protocol.
choices: Seek a customs union with the EU
Renegotiate the withdrawal deal
Prepare to leave without a deal

title: Net zero by 2050
context: Climate advisers say a net zero emissions target for 2050 is achievable. Business groups worry about the cost.
reality: In June 2019 Britain became the first major economy to legislate for net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, amending the Climate Change Act.
choices: Legislate net zero by 2050 with funding
Set a later or softer target
Keep the existing 80% target

title: Rising knife crime
context: Knife crime is at record levels and police numbers have fallen by about 20,000 since 2010.
reality: In July 2019 Boris Johnson pledged 20,000 more police officers in England and Wales by March 2023. The government reported the target met in 2023.
choices: Recruit thousands more police officers
Fund targeted violence reduction units
Leave priorities to police forces

title: Thomas Cook goes bust
context: The world's oldest travel firm faces collapse with around 150,000 British holidaymakers abroad. It asks for a state rescue.
reality: Thomas Cook collapsed in September 2019 after the government refused a bailout. The Civil Aviation Authority flew home about 140,000 customers, the largest peacetime repatriation.
choices: Bail out the travel company
Refuse a bailout but fly travellers home
Leave travellers to insurers

title: A new virus spreads
context: A new coronavirus is spreading rapidly and hospitals fear being overwhelmed. Scientific advisers urge drastic measures.
reality: On 23 March 2020 Boris Johnson ordered a national lockdown. Further lockdowns followed in November 2020 and January 2021; a public inquiry later criticised the delays.
choices: Impose a national lockdown
Use targeted restrictions and shielding
Rely on voluntary guidance

title: Saving jobs in lockdown
context: Lockdown shuts large parts of the economy overnight. Millions of jobs are at risk.
reality: The Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme paid 80% of wages up to £2,500 a month. It supported 11.7 million jobs before it closed at the end of September 2021.
choices: Pay most wages of furloughed staff
Offer targeted loans and grants
Leave firms to cope alone

title: Huawei and the 5G network
context: A Chinese firm supplies cheap 5G equipment. Allies warn of security risks; mobile operators warn of delays and costs.
reality: In January 2020 Huawei was capped at 35% of the network periphery. After new US sanctions, the government in July 2020 banned new Huawei kit and ordered its removal from 5G by 2027.
choices: Ban the vendor and fund alternatives
Cap its role outside the core network
Let operators choose their suppliers

title: The end of the transition
context: The Brexit transition period ends on 31 December. Talks with the EU stall over fishing, state aid and fair competition.
reality: On 24 December 2020 the UK and EU agreed the Trade and Cooperation Agreement, with zero tariffs and quotas on goods but new customs checks and paperwork.
choices: Extend the transition and seek closer ties
Sign a zero-tariff trade deal
Leave on WTO terms

title: A new pact in the Indo-Pacific
context: China's military power is growing. The United States and Australia discuss nuclear-powered submarines with Britain.
reality: AUKUS was announced in September 2021: Britain and the US agreed to help Australia acquire nuclear-powered submarines and to cooperate on advanced military technology.
choices: Join a security pact and invest heavily
Join with limited commitments
Stay out to protect trade with China

title: The fall of Kabul
context: US forces are withdrawing and the Taliban have taken Kabul. Thousands of Afghans who worked with Britain seek evacuation.
reality: Operation Pitting airlifted about 15,000 people from Kabul in August 2021. Resettlement schemes followed, but many eligible Afghans were left behind.
choices: Push allies to keep forces in place
Run a large evacuation and resettlement
Withdraw with minimal evacuations

title: Paying for social care
context: NHS backlogs are growing after the pandemic and social care is in crisis. A promise not to raise national insurance stands in the way.
reality: In September 2021 Boris Johnson announced a 1.25 percentage point Health and Social Care Levy on National Insurance. It took effect in April 2022 and was reversed that November.
choices: Raise national insurance to fund care
Fund care gradually through borrowing
Hold taxes and fund care from savings

title: Hosting the climate summit
context: Britain hosts the UN climate conference in Glasgow. It wants a deal to phase out coal and to cut emissions faster.
reality: The Glasgow Climate Pact of November 2021 was the first COP agreement to mention coal, but a late change pushed by India and China weakened 'phase-out' to 'phase-down'.
choices: Push for coal phase-out with climate finance
Broker a compromise on coal
Host without new pledges

title: Russia invades Ukraine
context: Russia launches a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Kyiv asks for weapons, and millions of refugees flee west.
reality: Britain supplied anti-tank weapons and other arms, imposed sweeping sanctions on Russia and launched the Homes for Ukraine scheme. It gave about £2.3bn of military aid in 2022.
choices: Supply arms and impose sweeping sanctions
Send aid and join targeted sanctions
Avoid steps that escalate the conflict

title: Energy bills explode
context: Gas prices have hit record highs. Household energy bills are set to rise far beyond what many families can afford.
reality: From October 2022 the Energy Price Guarantee capped a typical household bill at £2,500 a year, on top of a £400 bill discount. A windfall tax on oil and gas profits had been introduced in May.
source: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
choices: Cap bills for all households
Target support at the poorest households
Leave prices to the market

title: The mini-budget
context: The new government wants faster growth through large tax cuts funded by borrowing, at a time of high inflation and rising interest rates.
reality: Kwasi Kwarteng's September 2022 mini-budget announced about £45bn of unfunded tax cuts. Gilt markets slumped, the Bank of England intervened, Kwarteng was sacked and Liz Truss resigned within weeks.
choices: Fund energy support and invest within rules
Phase targeted cuts with funding
Cut taxes sharply, funded by borrowing

title: Compensating victims of infected blood
context: Thousands were infected with HIV and hepatitis through contaminated NHS blood products decades ago. Many have died waiting for compensation.
reality: In August 2022 the government agreed interim payments of £100,000 to around 4,000 infected people and bereaved partners. A full compensation scheme followed the inquiry's final report in 2024.
choices: Pay full compensation to all victims now
Pay interim sums and await the inquiry
Wait for the inquiry to finish

title: The Rwanda deportation plan
context: Small boat crossings remain high. The Supreme Court has ruled the plan to send asylum seekers to Rwanda unlawful.
reality: After the November 2023 ruling, Rishi Sunak signed a new treaty and passed the Safety of Rwanda Act 2024. No asylum seekers were forcibly removed, and the scheme was scrapped in July 2024.
choices: Override the courts by law and fund flights
Sign a new treaty and speed up processing
Drop the scheme

title: Fixing the Northern Ireland Protocol
context: Post-Brexit trade checks between Great Britain and Northern Ireland cause friction, and power-sharing has collapsed in protest.
reality: The Windsor Framework, agreed with the EU in February 2023, eased checks through a 'green lane' and added the 'Stormont brake'. Power-sharing resumed in February 2024.
choices: Align closely with EU rules across the UK
Negotiate a new framework with the EU
Override the protocol unilaterally

title: Strikes across the NHS
context: Nurses, ambulance staff and junior doctors walk out over pay eroded by inflation. Waiting lists reach record levels.
reality: Most NHS staff groups settled in 2023, but junior doctors kept striking. In July 2023 the government accepted pay review body awards of around 6%.
source: Department of Health and Social Care
choices: Fund the pay demands in full
Accept pay review awards, keep talking
Hold pay down to curb inflation

title: Slowing the green transition
context: Households face high living costs, and some politicians argue climate deadlines are too costly for families.
reality: In September 2023 Rishi Sunak delayed the ban on new petrol and diesel cars from 2030 to 2035 and softened the phase-out of gas boilers, while keeping the 2050 net zero target.
choices: Keep deadlines and fund the transition
Delay some targets, keep net zero
Scrap green targets and levies

title: The Post Office Horizon scandal
context: A television drama revives national outrage: hundreds of sub-postmasters were wrongly prosecuted because of a faulty IT system.
reality: After ITV's 'Mr Bates vs The Post Office' in January 2024, Parliament passed the Post Office (Horizon System) Offences Act 2024, quashing convictions en masse, and expanded compensation.
choices: Quash convictions by law and fund redress
Speed up appeals and compensation
Leave it to the courts

title: Riots after Southport
context: After three young girls are killed in a knife attack, misinformation online fuels riots, including attacks on mosques and hotels housing asylum seekers.
reality: Rioting spread across England and Northern Ireland in summer 2024. The government prioritised rapid arrests and fast-tracked prosecutions, with over 1,000 arrests and hundreds of prison sentences.
choices: Fund a standing national riot response force
Fast-track arrests and prosecutions
Leave policing to local forces

title: Prisons at bursting point
context: Prisons in England and Wales are almost full. Without action, courts may soon be unable to jail offenders.
reality: From September 2024 many prisoners were released after serving 40% of their sentence instead of 50%. Thousands left early while the government pledged 14,000 new prison places.
choices: Fund emergency prison places
Release some prisoners earlier
Leave it to courts and prison service

title: Filling the fiscal black hole
context: The new government says it has inherited a £22bn spending gap. Public services need money, but income tax and VAT rises have been ruled out.
reality: Rachel Reeves's October 2024 Budget raised taxes by about £40bn, chiefly by lifting employer National Insurance to 15% and cutting the threshold at which it is paid to £5,000.
choices: Raise taxes and invest in services
Raise some taxes and phase spending
Cut spending and avoid tax rises

title: A second tax-raising Budget
context: Weak growth and higher borrowing costs leave a hole in the public finances. Ministers face pressure to tackle child poverty without breaking tax pledges.
reality: Rachel Reeves's November 2025 Budget raised taxes by £26bn by 2029-30, mainly by freezing income tax thresholds until 2031, and scrapped the two-child benefit limit from April 2026.
choices: Raise taxes and lift child benefits
Freeze thresholds and phase measures
Cut spending to avoid tax rises

title: Welfare cuts and a backbench revolt
context: Sickness and disability benefit costs are rising fast. Planned cuts face a revolt by more than 100 government MPs.
reality: In July 2025 the government dropped its planned PIP eligibility changes pending a review led by Stephen Timms. The bill passed second reading with 49 Labour MPs voting against.
choices: Protect benefits and fund job support
Narrow the cuts and review disability benefits
Push the full cuts through

title: Rearming in a dangerous world
context: Washington demands that European allies spend far more on defence while Russia's war against Ukraine continues.
reality: In February 2025 Keir Starmer pledged defence spending of 2.5% of GDP by 2027, funded by cutting aid to 0.3% of GNI. At the NATO summit in June he backed 5% by 2035, including 3.5% on core defence.
choices: Raise defence spending fast, fund by taxes
Raise it gradually, fund by cutting aid
Keep defence spending near current levels

title: Asylum hotels and small boats
context: Small boat arrivals stay high and hotels housing asylum seekers spark protests in several towns. Pressure for tougher rules grows.
reality: Protests at an Epping asylum hotel spread in summer 2025. Britain agreed a 'one in, one out' returns pilot with France and in November proposed temporary refugee status and a 20-year wait for settlement.
choices: Fund faster processing and new housing
Agree returns deals and tighten rules
Leave asylum housing to councils

title: War with Iran and British bases
context: The United States and Israel have struck Iran, which retaliates and threatens shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Washington asks to use British bases.
reality: After the war began on 28 February 2026, Keir Starmer let the US use British bases for defensive operations and, from March, strikes on missile sites targeting shipping, but kept Britain out of offensive action.
choices: Join US operations with British forces
Allow limited defensive use of bases
Refuse any use of British bases

title: Energy bills rise again
context: War in the Gulf has driven up oil and gas prices. Household energy bills and fuel costs are climbing again.
reality: In July 2026 the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, scrapped VAT on household electricity from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027, worth about £45 a year, as Ofgem's October price cap rose by about 4%.
choices: Fund broad support for all energy bills
Scrap VAT on electricity bills only
Leave bills to the price cap

title: Funding the armed forces
context: A ten-year defence investment plan is long overdue. Military chiefs say the money on offer falls short, while other departments face cuts to pay for defence.
reality: In June 2026 Defence Secretary John Healey resigned, saying the funding settlement for the Defence Investment Plan fell well short of what the forces needed. Keir Starmer announced his own resignation later that month.
choices: Fund the forces' full investment plan
Agree a constrained ten-year plan
Hold defence budgets flat

title: The digital ID climbdown
context: A national digital ID, required to prove the right to work, faces a petition signed by millions and opposition from across the political spectrum.
reality: Announced in September 2025, the scheme's mandatory right-to-work element was dropped in January 2026. In July 2026 Andy Burnham's government cancelled the programme to help fund a cut in VAT on electricity.
choices: Build a mandatory national digital ID
Offer a voluntary digital ID
Scrap the digital ID programme
